title: How do you answer "Tell me about a time you led a team through difficulty"?
description: How to structure a leadership story for consulting interviews, with weak and strong example answers and how to handle deep follow-up questions.
hook: You answer "Tell me about a time you led a team through difficulty" with one specific story where something real went wrong, then spend most of your time on the decisions you personally made, how you handled people who disagreed, and the measurable result. Leadership questions are where interviewers dig deepest, especially in McKinsey's Personal Experience Interview. They want to know what you did when things got hard, not what the team achieved.
body:
What the interviewer is testing

Leadership in a consulting interview is not about job titles. You can lead from any seat. The interviewer is looking for evidence that you noticed a problem, made a call, brought people with you and changed the outcome. In practice they listen for three things:

  • A real difficulty, not just a busy week. A team falling apart, a deadline that could not be met, a conflict.
  • A decision only you made, ideally involving a trade-off.
  • How you handled people, especially anyone who disagreed.

A weak answer

In my final-year project, our team was behind schedule. We worked really hard together, had more meetings and in the end we delivered on time and got a good grade.

Why it falls short: it says "we" throughout, gives no detail on the difficulty or the decisions, and shows nothing about the speaker as a leader. "More meetings" is not a leadership action.

A strong answer

This example is illustrative; use the shape with your own story.

Six weeks before our final project deadline, two of our five team members stopped turning up, and we were two weeks behind. Rather than escalate to our supervisor, I spoke to each of them one to one. One was overwhelmed by a part-time job; the other had lost confidence after his section was criticised. I re-split the work so the first owned a smaller, self-contained piece she could do at weekends, and paired the second with me on the data analysis. I replaced our long weekly meeting with a 15-minute check-in twice a week, so problems came up early. We delivered on time and got the highest mark in the cohort. What I learned is to find out why someone has stopped before deciding they don't care.

Why it works: the difficulty is concrete, the actions are specific and in the first person, there is a choice (talk first rather than escalate), the result is measurable, and the lesson is a habit. It is also ready for follow-ups like "Why did you choose that split?"

Show the trade-off you accepted

The strongest leadership stories include a decision with a cost. Here is a second illustrative example, summarised:

A five-person team was preparing a client presentation when the customer data arrived two weeks late, leaving one week and three unfinished workstreams. Instead of asking everyone to work harder, the candidate met each workstream lead, separated essential analysis from nice-to-have, and agreed with the client which questions had to be answered for the decision. Two teammates wanted to keep every chart. The candidate explained the deadline risk, invited them to challenge the priorities, and moved two people onto checking the core numbers. The team delivered the essential recommendation on time and scheduled the rest as a follow-up.

The important details are what the candidate decided, how the disagreement was handled, and which trade-off was accepted: less analysis, delivered on time and checked. Claiming credit for all five people's work would undermine it.

Prepare for the follow-ups

Expect the interviewer to probe. Practise answering:

  • "Why did you choose that approach over the alternatives?"
  • "What exactly did you say to the people who disagreed?"
  • "How did you know the reduced scope was acceptable?"
  • "What would you do differently?"

If you cannot answer these comfortably, use a different story. A smaller, genuine incident you remember in detail beats an impressive but vague one.

Common mistakes

  • "We" for everything. Use "we" for the team's situation and "I" for your actions.
  • No real difficulty. If nothing was at risk, there was nothing to lead through.
  • The hero story. You alone saved the day while others were useless. It sounds implausible and unkind. Show how you got the best out of people.
  • Too much set-up. Keep the situation to two or three sentences and spend at least half your time on actions.
  • A vague lesson. "Communication is key" is not a lesson. Name what you now do differently.

Try it now

1. Turn this into a leadership action: "We had lots of disagreements, but we worked through them."

Show the answer

Name the disagreement and what you did: "Two of us wanted to target students and two wanted families. I suggested we each spend a day testing our idea with ten real customers, and agreed in advance that the data would decide. Families won, and the two who'd argued for students led the next phase."

2. Your story has a great result but the difficulty was mild. What should you do?

Show the answer

Use it for an impact or achievement question instead, and find a different story for leadership, one where something went wrong or people disagreed. Leadership is shown by what you did under pressure.

3. Write the action part of your own leadership story in four sentences, each starting with "I".

Show the answer

Check that each sentence is something you did, not something that happened, and that at least one shows a choice between options. If two sentences describe effort ("I worked late"), replace them with decisions.

Where to practise next

Build the rest of your story bank with the fit interview guide. If you are applying to McKinsey, the McKinsey interview process guide explains how deep the follow-ups go. Leadership stories overlap with persuading without authority, so prepare both, then ask a partner to grill you using the follow-ups above; the guide to practising with a partner shows how.
